title: The Rite of Spring Is One of My Favorite Scores of All Time
description: A look into Stravinsky's most famous (and infamous) work.
__content: # The Rite of Spring Is One of My Favorite Scores of All Time *The following post may contain copyrighted material for the purpose of commentary, criticism, and education. No ownership is implied by that use.* *Cover Image: By Nicholas Roerich - from State Russian Museum, St. Petersburg at http://www.roerich.org/images/paintings/701809_043.jpg, Public Domain, Link* # Background The Rite of Spring has been described as one of the most influential works of the modern era. Many have argued that it had completely transformed the trajectory of modern classical music into what we know it as today. Far from the dainty, refined ballet of the time, it depicts scenes of Pagan life in Russia, as a tribe celebrates the arrival of spring. Later, the tribe elects a maiden to sacrifice herself through dance to appease the gods, promising another bountiful year. The instrumentation is enormous, even by today's standards, calling for a staggering twenty wind players, eighteen brass players, a large selection of percussion instruments, and as many string players as the company could afford. The set design involved heavy, peasant clothes, with none of the elegance of typical ballet dresses. The choreography broke nearly all rules of traditional ballet, calling for heavy-footed rhythms, awkward jumps and leaps, and several instances where dancers intentionally fight the rhythm rather than dance to it. In short, the scoring and choreography were like nothing the audience of the day had seen before. These elements were combined together by Igor Stravinsky and his partners under the Ballets Russes. The Ballets Russes, founded in 1909, performed several ballets written by composers across Europe. They specialized in both older and newer ballet works, many of which gained polarizing reputations. The director of the group, Sergei Diaghilev, had already gained substantial fame at the time of the Rite of Spring's premiere in 1913. Stravinsky, by comparison, was hardly known at all until the success of The Firebird, and gained much of his fame through his ballets. Indeed, it's likely that much of his fame was won through The Rite of Spring alone. Vaslav Nijinsky handled the choreography, and Nicholas Roerich handled cultural research, set design, and gave Stravinsky perspective on Russian life before Christianity. I highly recommend you check out any of these two videos if you would like more background on the score, choreography, or the Ballets Russes. These videos are shorter introductions to The Rite of Spring with less overall depth. Be warned: some of the information in those videos comes from accounts that have since been **disputed or even debunked**. Check out "Further Exploration" for more information. - [TED-ED](https://youtu.be/8FXA_8LR2IM?si=s-7BEtH3k5ZUFhGe) - [Classics Explained](https://youtu.be/6UKrmPoJv-k?si=ll77l7wlJUnGuN0a) # The Music I highly recommend that you listen to at least a portion of The Rite of Spring before reading my thoughts. The score+audio version is the one that I watched, and it also happens to have some of the best orchestral brass playing I've ever experienced. There is also a recording by the London Symphony Orchestra, as well as a recording of a 1987 performance by the Joffrey Ballet. - [Score + Audio](https://youtu.be/rP42C-4zL3w?si=6mGz4i4Jiw1YJSo1) - [London Symphony Orchestra](https://youtu.be/EkwqPJZe8ms?si=Ek086xf5UmygiNvg) - [Joffrey Ballet 1987](https://youtu.be/jo4sf2wT0wU?si=JtMEbIj6wUh3h4yT) # My Thoughts I had listened to part of this score a few years back, in fact, but was unable to finish it. I was very unprepared for the brutalist harmony and chaos that ensued during "The Ritual of Abduction," and could not handle the rest of the music. Coming back to this, having listened to more experimental harmony and modern music theory, has allowed me to endure the entire performance. I've also come to appreciate the piece substantially more in the process. Despite its apparent barbarism, it's actually quite a refined, modern piece. The chaos exists, yes, but it's carefully crafted. Stravinsky knew how to take advantage of the massive orchestra and extended techniques of certain instruments to create otherworldly effects. It seems random or arbitrary at times, but many passages lose their effect without the careful emphasis of certain harmonies, melodies, and colors. To me, Stravinsky demonstrates that he can orchestrate a passage just as effectively as Ravel, though with a completely different meaning and individual style. That's why I find this piece so compelling. It's nothing like any piece that came before, and even today, it stands on its own pillars of creativity, cleverness, skill, and imagination. # Top 5 Favorite Moments **VOLUME WARNING**: Some of these passages may start extremely loud. Please adjust your volume now in anticipation. Also, these entries are in no particular order. ## [08:03](https://youtu.be/rP42C-4zL3w?si=DmQ25XiSCi-eyzDN&t=483): The Khorovod After the ferocity and brutality of the Ritual of Abduction, the music subsides into the Spring Rounds. Trilling flutes set the stage for an ethereal melody on two clarinet auxiliaries: the E♭ clarinet and the bass clarinet. Scoring the E♭ clarinet for a slow, soft melody is incredibly creative. Much of the typical melodies and harmonies given to the E♭ clarinet involve loud, piercing passages that often have a harsh edge. However, Stravinsky shows the capability of the instrument beyond simple conventions. Adding the bass clarinet to the melody two octaves lower gives stability to the line and smooths out some of the higher harmonics of the E♭ clarinet. The result is a beautiful yet eerie melody, offering some relief to the listener while maintaining the picture of an ancient, unrefined world. Eventually, the melody is repeated, this time with alto flute substituting bass clarinet and with a slightly different key center. I appreciate the variation in the repetition, but still find the original melody to be more impactful. ## [25:08](https://youtu.be/rP42C-4zL3w?si=C35EGrnDLtVjNowA&t=1508): The Timpani Solo During one of the most intense parts of the score, the Glorification of the Chosen One, there is a sudden drop after a furious slash from the trumpets. In this instant, it's the timpani that's given the role of the soloist, guiding the orchestra in a 2/4 pattern while the orchestra dances expectantly around it. Instances of percussion being the primary voice of the orchestra are very rare in classical music. Their traditional role has always been to support and embellish the orchestra, not to dominate it. Stravinsky throws the idea out the window during this passage, and to great effect. The tension between the rhythm of the timpani and the violins builds for several bars, allowing the anxiety of the passage to reach a breaking point. After the timpani solo, the high horns snarl out a melody alongside woodwinds, which is answered by a call on trumpets and trombones. I love how the latter instruments utilize the consonant and dissonant qualities of major seconds to create a bright, punchy sound that completely swallows the orchestra. Combined with swirling woodwinds and strings, the texture is incredibly commanding. The passage ends in a triumphant melody on brass, followed by a return to an earlier section. ## [26:44](https://youtu.be/rP42C-4zL3w?si=QDjN0uIOhSF6QvaQ&t=1604): English Horn + Alto Flute Duet Shortly after the Glorification of the Chosen One, the Ritual Action of the Ancestors follows. I love the tension that's built through the tiptoe-like texture of the pizzicato strings, staccato horns, and the percussion. In particular, the combination of timpani and tambourine is very unusual, but it offers both weight and articulation that keeps the audience on the edge. The English horn solo is a beautiful example of how the instrument can deliver a sly, menacing quality, rather than being restricted to only the most solemn, expressive solos. The density and tightness of the timbre give a strange, uncouth background to the alto flute solo. The alto flute in its low register balances well with the subtler English horn, the restrained brass horns, and the strings. It dances around the English horn suspiciously, although I find that this solo is more reminiscent of jazz music than anything else, oddly enough. A second alto flute solo follows afterwards, keeping the tension high, though I find the English horn and flute duet to be one of the most compelling parts of the piece. ## [30:34](https://youtu.be/rP42C-4zL3w?si=DMKkCQ0OMctGfpqX&t=1834): Stuttering Heartbeat Nearing the end of the piece, the chosen one dances herself to death. After a crashing tutti passage, the music suddenly gets quiet. Strings, bassoons, and horns keep the energy and tension pulled tight. I love that the horns are given double notes while the rest of the orchestra is given single notes. It creates a pulsing effect, almost as if the chosen one's heart is beating so strongly the music itself is affected by it. In my opinion, the trombone soli is what makes this passage so special. Even at a modest forte dynamic, the muted trombones can cut through the texture and pierce straight into the listener's ear. The answer in trumpets is even more emphatic. This section is followed by the original rhythm, which eventually cuts out the horns and bassoons and pushes the strings to a much louder dynamic. The original quintuplet idea that first appeared in the trombone soli is repeated in piccolo, E♭ clarinet, and D trumpet. The sound is thin, bright, and extremely abrasive. Then the same motif is repeated with trumpets, E♭ clarinet, and horns, and eventually leads to a large tutti section that continues the rhythm. ## [08:33](https://youtu.be/rP42C-4zL3w?si=bbAGDVZz56_sHkjv&t=513): Section B of Spring Rounds After the E♭ and bass clarinet duo that introduced the spring rounds, a new modal theme is introduced with a heavy bassline and strong syncopations. I love the warmth and depth that the orchestra gives here; it emulates with great effect the warmth and sincerity that the Earth provides at the arrival of spring. This bassline is interrupted by small melodies on oboe and bassoon, harmonized by clarinets and violins. I've used both double reeds for melodies a few times in my own works, and I love the smoothness and focus that you get out of the combination. The main melody, however, is played on a quartet of horns, violas, and flutes. Stravinsky changes the instrumentation of the melodies a few times to create different colors, taking advantage of the differing sonorities of horns, flutes, and violas. If the horns are able to play the notes above the staff at a soft dynamic, they can exude a beautifully smooth, stately sound. The violas and flutes, by contrast, tend to use a lot of vibrato, and have an overall warmer sound in their middle to low register. The contrast between the stately horns and expressive violas and flutes are combined give a wonderful ceremonial quality. At such a soft dynamic, the flutes blend much better with the other quartets and can be heard alongside them. After more oboe and bassoon duets, the texture expands into a massive tutti. All the upper strings, flutes, and clarinets thrash away with the first horn on the initial melody, and Stravinsky introduces an extremely dissonant reharmonization in the rest of the orchestra. I find it incredible that the first horn is never doubled by another horn or trumpet during the entire tutti; the horn's high register is so loud that it needs almost no support. My favorite part in all of this is the interjections by heavy brass. The volume and savagery that the trumpets and trombones are able to pump out are incredibly powerful, so much so that the top E♭ of the melody can be completely swamped. The effect is incredible, and gave me goosebumps the first time I listened to it. # Conclusion I'm very thankful that I was able to come back to this piece to listen to it after not being able to get through it before. I'm pretty certain that the vast majority of people wouldn't enjoy this piece for many reasons, whether its the harsh harmony, the uncouth rhythm, or just the lack of any sense of lasting closure or peace. This piece isn't really meant for the typical listener of classical music, let alone any genre of music. The Firebird and Petrushka may be the more popular ballets, and I do find those ones to be enjoyable too. But, I would recommend listening to at least a little bit of The Rite of Spring if you get the chance. The skills Stravinsky displayed in orchestration, tone painting, and overall imagination are incredible; far beyond that of many composers in my opinion. It's over a century old, yet the sophistication and modernity of the piece make it timeless. # Further Exploration This score analysis series by Thomas Goss also contains interviews and historical background, the latter of which has been **more thoroughly verified**. In particular, [one of the last videos](https://youtu.be/0x7znDvDLww?si=oydkaBKnfej6x5Cl) goes in-depth about the controversies and false accounts of The Rite of Spring. [OrchestrationOnline: Analysis by Thomas Goss](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL7C2C0FC5318C4861)
